mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding can last anywhere from five to ten years in many cases, though this is highly individual and depends on factors such as oral hygiene, diet, bite pattern, and lifestyle habits. Some patients find their bonding remains in good condition beyond this range with attentive maintenance, while others may require earlier repair or replacement. There is no guaranteed lifespan, and your dentist is best placed to give you a realistic expectation based on your specific clinical circumstances during a face-to-face assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can composite bonding stain over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, composite resin can absorb pigments from food and drink over time, which may lead to gradual discolouration. Common contributors include coffee, tea, red wine, and strongly coloured sauces. Unlike natural enamel, composite cannot be whitened using standard tooth whitening treatments, so prevention is more effective than correction. Regular professional polishing at hygiene appointments can help manage surface staining, and rinsing with water after consuming pigmented foods or drinks may help reduce absorption.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible to repair composite bonding if it chips?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes. A small chip or fracture in a composite bonded restoration can often be repaired relatively straightforwardly during a dental appointment. Your dentist will assess the extent of the damage and determine whether direct repair is suitable or whether the restoration requires replacement. It is important not to leave a chipped restoration unaddressed, as rough edges can irritate the tongue or gum tissue, and exposed tooth structure may become more vulnerable. Seeking professional assessment promptly is always advisable.

mainEntity.name: Does teeth grinding affect composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, bruxism (teeth grinding and clenching) can have a significant impact on composite bonding life. The forces generated during grinding can exceed those of normal chewing many times over, accelerating wear and increasing the risk of chipping or fracture. If your dentist identifies signs of bruxism during an examination, they may recommend a custom-fitted occlusal splint (night guard) to protect both your natural teeth and any bonded restorations. Addressing bruxism is an important part of protecting cosmetic dental work.

mainEntity.name: Does composite bonding require special cleaning products?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding does not typically require specialist cleaning products, but certain standard products are better suited to protecting the material. Non-abrasive fluoride toothpastes are preferable to whitening or gritty formulations, which can dull the surface of composite resin over time. Alcohol-free mouthwashes are generally recommended over alcohol-containing varieties. A soft-bristled toothbrush is advisable to minimise surface abrasion. Your dental team can offer personalised product recommendations based on your specific restorations and oral health needs at your next appointment.

mainEntity.name: Can composite bonding be replaced if it deteriorates?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, composite bonding can generally be replaced when it reaches the end of its functional or aesthetic lifespan. The process typically involves removing the existing composite material and applying fresh resin, which is then sculpted and polished to match your smile. Because composite bonding is a relatively minimally invasive treatment, replacement is generally straightforward in most clinical situations. However, the suitability of replacement — and whether alternative options such as porcelain veneers might be more appropriate at that stage — should be discussed with your dentist during a clinical consultation.
